query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In ambient environments, the frictional loading on HEA coatings induces two cooperative phenomena—a dynamic formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer via shear‐driven grain refinement and a concurrent development of a thin, coherent oxide (glaze) film—that together stabilize the refined microstructure and inhibit crack propagation. In contrast, in inert (e.g., UHV) conditions where only grain refinement occurs, the absence of the oxide film leads to inferior wear resistance despite low friction coefficients.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) produced with a relatively coarse initial grain structure via laser additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Perform systematic pin-on-disk wear tests while varying the ambient oxygen level: compare tests in a fully inert (UHV) environment, in ambient air, and in a controlled oxygen-enriched atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Normal loads and sliding speeds spanning low to moderate regimes (e.g., 1–10 mm/s sliding speed, moderate loads), temperatures maintained below ~400 °C, and consistent test durations to ensure reproducibility.
generation.structural_mediator: A dynamically evolved ultra-nanocrystalline tribo-layer that becomes further stabilized by the formation of a thin, continuous oxide film on the wear surface.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding in ambient conditions, frictional energy generates rapid shear-induced grain refinement, producing an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer. Simultaneously, the reactive elements in the HEA form a thin oxide film that coats the refined grains, reinforcing the grain boundaries and mitigating crack initiation or propagation. In inert environments, while grain refinement (and its associated inverse Hall–Petch softening) occurs, the lack of this stabilizing oxide layer leads to higher wear rates despite lower friction coefficients.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples tested in ambient or mildly oxygen-enriched conditions will show lower specific wear rates and improved surface integrity (e.g., fewer cracks, more stable refined layer) compared to inert conditions. Extremely oxygen-rich conditions, however, may yield overly thick or brittle oxides and thus compromise wear performance. Thus, an optimum oxygen partial pressure exists where the synergistic effect is maximized.
generation.baseline: Wear tests conducted in an inert (UHV) environment where only shear‐induced grain refinement occurs without any oxide layer formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEA coatings with elements prone to rapid oxide formation at moderate temperatures. It may not extend to conditions with extreme oxidation (e.g., very high temperatures or excessively oxygen-rich environments) where oxide layers become too thick or brittle.
generation.uncertainty: The study combines evidence of dynamic grain refinement and inverse Hall–Petch behavior in inert environments (PMC7311485::web::012::results_and_discussion) with findings on beneficial glaze layer formation in ambient CCAs (PMC10241162::web::003::introduction). What is new is the proposition that in HEA coatings the simultaneous formation and stabilization of a refined grain structure by a thin oxide film can cooperatively enhance wear resistance—a synergistic effect not directly tested before. Uncertainty remains regarding the optimal oxygen level that produces such a beneficial oxide film without causing detrimental thickening or brittleness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical HEA-coated samples and conduct pin-on-disk wear tests under three atmospheres: (1) UHV (inert), (2) ambient air, and (3) oxygen-enriched (controlled higher oxygen partial pressure). For each atmosphere, use a spectrum of sliding speeds and applied loads. After testing, use cross-sectional SEM/TEM coupled with EDS to measure the grain size distribution in the top tribo-layer, the thickness and continuity of any oxide film, and quantify the wear rate and friction coefficient.
measurements: Grain size distribution of the near-surface layer (via TEM)
Oxide layer thickness and continuity (via cross-sectional SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If tests under ambient or oxygen-enriched conditions do not display a lower wear rate (or show no significant improvement in surface stabilization despite oxide formation) compared to inert conditions—i.e., if the oxide film does not correlate with a stabilized ultra-nanocrystalline microstructure and reduced cracking—then the hypothesis is falsified.

This work studied an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy that was manufactured using a laser-based consolidation additive manufacturing process. We showed that low friction and high wear resistance are achievable with bare high entropy alloys in inert environments. These characteristics are linked to the shear-induced formation of a highly refined, near-amorphous surface film that exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior. The detrimental role of environments, specifically those that result in oxidation, was mitigated by tribological testing in a UHV environment. A newly proposed amorphization model was used to accurately predict the grain size-dependent shear strength, and thus friction coefficient.
